query: Eutectic high-entropy alloys contain dual-phase lamellar colonies with numerous internal boundaries, where microcracking can initiate and lead to catastrophic damage during room-temperature tensile deformation. Conventional processing commonly raises strength at the expense of ductility, while the wide range of previously proposed microstructural-design and processing strategies has not eliminated room-temperature brittleness and limited tensile ductility. Under these constraints, what single intervention could improve both strength and room-temperature tensile ductility? State one testable hypothesis that identifies the intervention, explains its mechanism, predicts outcomes relative to the unmodified lamellar-colony baseline, defines its boundary conditions, cites supporting prior evidence, and proposes an experiment whose result would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: Introducing a trace amount of Nb into a eutectic high‐entropy alloy will promote Nb segregation to the internal boundaries of dual‐phase lamellar colonies, leading to the in situ formation of coherent nanoscale precipitates. These precipitates will both impede dislocation motion and reinforce internal boundaries, thereby improving tensile strength and ductility under room‐temperature deformation compared to the unmodified alloy.
generation.material_initial_state: A eutectic high‐entropy alloy with dual‐phase lamellar colonies containing numerous internal boundaries prone to microcrack initiation during room‐temperature tensile deformation.
generation.intervention: Introduce a trace concentration of Nb as a microalloying element.
generation.conditions: Room-temperature tensile deformation with processing that preserves the lamellar colony structure; Nb concentration must be controlled within a narrow window to ensure coherent precipitate formation.
generation.structural_mediator: Nanoscale, coherent precipitates formed at internal boundaries.
generation.mechanism: Nb segregates to the internal boundaries and triggers the formation of coherent precipitates. These precipitates obstruct dislocation movement (enhancing strength) and stabilize the boundaries to delay or prevent microcrack initiation (enhancing ductility).
generation.predicted_outcome: Relative to the unmodified alloy, the Nb-added alloy will exhibit increased tensile strength due to precipitation hardening and improved ductility due to greater resistance to microcrack nucleation under room-temperature tension.
generation.baseline: Eutectic high‐entropy alloy with conventional dual‐phase lamellar colonies where internal boundaries act as stress concentrators leading to early microcrack initiation and brittle failure during tensile deformation.
generation.boundary: The beneficial effect is expected only if the Nb content is within an optimized narrow range that promotes coherent nanoscale precipitate formation without leading to deleterious phase embrittlement or loss of the desirable lamellar morphology.
generation.uncertainty: The exact quantitative improvements in strength and ductility and the specific segregation behavior of Nb in this alloy system are uncertain and require experimental validation.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of samples from the same eutectic high‐entropy alloy: one set with the trace Nb addition at the optimized concentration and a control set without Nb. Characterize the internal boundaries using TEM and atom probe tomography to detect the presence and coherency of nanoscale precipitates, then perform standardized room-temperature tensile tests to quantify mechanical properties.
measurements: Size, distribution, and coherency of interfacial precipitates (via TEM/APT)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If Nb-added samples do not form coherent nanoscale precipitates at the internal boundaries or if there is no statistically significant simultaneous improvement in tensile strength and ductility (or if performance deteriorates compared to the baseline), then the hypothesis is falsified.

cited_evidence.kind: web:The role of phase boundary in second phase strengthening
cited_evidence.text: It is a traditional method to strengthen alloys by introducing internal boundaries in order to impede the motion of dislocations. Unlike coherent twin boundaries with low excess energies, grain boundaries and phase boundaries are regarded as major strengthening agents for metallic materials because they are more effective in resisting dislocation penetration. In this study, the phase boundaries were produced through the eutectic reaction during the preparation of dual-phase AlCoCrFeNi2.1 HEA. Thereby plenty of phase boundaries contained in this HEA were semi-coherent due to the low energy features. Given that interfacial strength increases with the decrease of coherency, phase boundaries of semi-coherence prepared in eutectic dual-phase HEAs were observed to be strong enough to accommodate high stress due to their chemically disordered features, as proved by the HAADF-STEM observation (Fig. 3b) and in-situ straining experiments. Such strong phase boundaries were essential to achieving compatibility of interphase deformations through enhancing the strength of FCC phases by work hardening effects so as to commence dislocation glide in BCC phases.

Realizing improved strength–ductility synergy in eutectic alloys acting as in situ composite materials remains a challenge in conventional eutectic systems, which is why eutectic high-entropy alloys (EHEAs), a newly-emerging multi-principal-element eutectic category, may offer wider in situ composite possibilities. Here, we use an AlCoCrFeNi2.1 EHEA to engineer an ultrafine-grained duplex microstructure that deliberately inherits its composite lamellar nature by tailored thermo-mechanical processing to achieve property combinations which are not accessible to previously-reported reinforcement methodologies. The as-prepared samples exhibit hierarchically-structural heterogeneity due to phase decomposition, and the improved mechanical response during deformation is attributed to both a two-hierarchical constraint effect and a self-generated microcrack-arresting mechanism. This work provides a pathway for strengthening eutectic alloys and widens the design toolbox for high-performance materials based upon EHEAs. frame.system: Eutectic high‐entropy alloys composed of dual‐phase lamellar colonies with numerous internal boundaries that serve as potential crack-nucleation sites.
frame.goal: Simultaneously enhance strength and room-temperature tensile ductility by mitigating microcrack initiation and propagation.
frame.limitation: Conventional processing strategies improve strength at the expense of ductility, and previous microstructural-design interventions have not overcome room-temperature brittleness.
root_cause_cues: catastrophic damage during room-temperature tensile deformation
constraints: Only a single intervention is allowed
The intervention must improve both strength and ductility without altering the overall lamellar morphology detrimentally
prior_attempts: Conventional processing methods that increase strength while sacrificing ductility
A wide range of microstructural-design or processing strategies that have not fully eliminated brittle behavior
frame.understanding: The hypothesis seeks to elucidate how targeted interfacial engineering (via trace microalloying) can modify internal boundary chemistry and structure to both impede dislocation motion (thus strengthening) and act as barriers to microcrack initiation (thus enhancing ductility).
frame.hypothesis: Introducing a small, optimally tuned concentration of a microalloying element (e.g., Nb or a similar element known to segregate at grain boundaries) into the eutectic high‐entropy alloy will induce the formation of nanoscale, coherent interfacial precipitates at the internal boundaries. This interfacial modification will yield dual benefits: (1) it will obstruct dislocation motion, thereby contributing to higher strength, and (2) by stabilizing and strengthening the internal boundaries, it will retard microcrack nucleation and propagation, resulting in improved ductility relative to the baseline lamellar colony structure. The intervention should be effective under room-temperature tensile deformation and within a narrow concentration window where the precipitates are coherent and uniformly distributed. This hypothesis is supported by prior evidence in conventional alloys where boundary segregation of microalloying elements improved toughness without sacrificing strength. An experiment to test—and potentially falsify—this hypothesis would involve preparing alloy samples with and without the microalloying addition, characterizing the resultant interfacial phases using TEM and atom probe tomography, and performing standardized room-temperature tensile tests. A failure to observe the predicted formation of coherent nanoscale precipitates or the absence of an improved strength-ductility balance relative to the unmodified alloy would falsify the hypothesis.

decision.trend: Early studies in eutectic high‐entropy alloys established the promising combination of dual‐phase lamellar microstructures (typically fcc/B2 or similar arrangements) to achieve high strength and ductility. Initial works (e.g., PMC4145285) demonstrated that eutectic alloys cast into fine lamellar arrangements can inherently provide a balance between hard and soft phases, but the intrinsic network of internal boundaries still poses a risk for microcrack initiation under room-temperature tension. Subsequent efforts (PMC6353877, PMC6687781) employed thermomechanical treatments and processing routes to refine the lamellar architecture and even create heterogeneous microstructures, thereby enhancing strength and ductility via mechanisms such as phase decomposition and dual structure-composition heterogeneities. Despite these successes, none of these processing-oriented interventions directly addressed the fundamental weakness of the internal interfaces that lead to microcracking.
decision.unsolved: While processing and microstructural design strategies have led to improvements in strength–ductility synergy, the critical issue of unstable internal boundaries that nucleate microcracks during room-temperature tensile deformation persists. The proposed interventions have not eliminated the brittleness because they do not fundamentally alter the chemistry or stability of the interfacial regions within the lamellar colonies.
decision.lever: Introduce a trace amount of a microalloying element (e.g., Nb) optimized to segregate at internal boundaries, thereby inducing the in-situ formation of coherent nanoscale precipitates
decision.why: This intervention logically follows the trend from processing‐based improvements—by now retaining the advantageous lamellar morphology, the approach targets the root cause (internal boundary instability) via chemical and interfacial engineering. Prior evidence from conventional alloy systems indicates that such microalloying can both obstruct dislocation motion (increasing strength) and stabilize boundaries (retarding microcrack initiation), making it a single, testable intervention that addresses both strength and ductility simultaneously under room-temperature tension.
